result:
A race condition is when the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of two or more processes touching the same resource, so the result is sometimes right and sometimes corrupted. In a log file, this shows up as interleaved or garbled lines when two scripts write at once.

To avoid it, take an exclusive lock around the write with `flock`:

```sh
{
  flock -x 9
  echo "$(date -Is) $$ something happened" >&9
} 9>>/var/log/shared.log
```

Every writer must use the same locking, since `flock` is advisory and does nothing against a process that ignores it. The lock is released automatically when the block ends, even if the script dies.

A single short `echo ... >> file` is already safe in practice on a local filesystem, because append mode makes each write land at the end of the file in one piece. You need the lock when an entry takes several writes (multi-line output, a command's piped output), or when the file is on NFS, where neither append atomicity nor `flock` is reliable.
